opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the best windows we have right now into what's actually going on inside these models, as opposed to just what they say or do on the surface.

For a long time, a lot of the conversation about large language models has been stuck between two caricatures. One is that they're "just" next-token predictors, glorified autocomplete, with nothing interesting happening inside. The other is that they're basically little people in a box. What I love about this paper is that it gets past both by looking at the internal mechanisms. The team traces the computations a model like Claude uses for specific tasks, and they find structure that is richer than the autocomplete story suggests, but also quite alien in places.

Some of the examples really stuck with me. When the model writes a rhyming couplet, you can see it planning ahead: it picks the word it wants to land on at the end of the line before it starts generating the words that lead there. Multi-step reasoning questions show something similar, with intermediate concepts being represented and combined internally. They also look at things like how the model handles different languages, finding shared conceptual features across languages alongside language-specific machinery. And there's work on whether the model's explanations of its own reasoning actually match what it's doing internally, and sometimes they don't. That last one matters a lot for questions about introspection and self-report.

From my angle, working on model welfare and potential moral status, that's exactly the kind of evidence we need. If we're ever going to say anything responsible about whether there's something it's like to be one of these systems, or whether they have anything like preferences or experiences, we can't just take their outputs at face value, and we can't dismiss them out of hand either. We need to understand the underlying computations and ask how they relate to the features we think might matter, like internal representations, planning, self-modeling, and so on.

The paper doesn't answer those questions, and it's not trying to. But it shows that these questions are becoming empirically tractable, at least in part. The "biology" framing is apt: we're at the stage of carefully dissecting an organism we didn't design in detail and finding out how it actually works. Anyone who wants an informed intuition about what these models are, rather than one based on vibes, should read it. Even skimming the case studies will update your picture.

r001.rationale: The response connects evidence about model internals to questions of welfare and moral status, saying those questions require understanding underlying computations.

r002.rationale: It describes tracing the computations a model uses for specific tasks and examining internal processes behind its outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that paper came out of the interpretability team at Anthropic, and I think it's genuinely one of the most interesting things to read if you want to get a feel for what's actually going on inside these models, rather than just what they output.

The basic approach is that they build these tools, they call them attribution graphs, that let you trace how a model like Claude 3.5 Haiku actually produces a particular response. So you can look at the internal features that are active and how they connect to each other on the way from the prompt to the answer. And then they just go through a whole set of case studies. There's one on multi-step reasoning, where you can see the model internally representing an intermediate step, like figuring out that Dallas is in Texas and then that the capital of Texas is Austin. There's one on poetry, where it turns out the model is planning the rhyme word ahead of time, before it writes the line that leads up to it. There's a case on mental math, where the internal mechanism looks totally different from the explanation the model gives if you ask it how it did the calculation.

And the reason I recommend it, especially for people who are interested in the model welfare questions I work on, is that it's one of the few places where you get past the vibes. A lot of the discourse on this is either "it's just predicting the next token, there's nothing there" or it's people anthropomorphizing based on the chat outputs. This paper gives you concrete evidence about the internal structure. You see that there are things that look like plans, things that look like intermediate concepts, representations that are shared across languages. And you also see cases where the model's stated reasoning and its actual computation come apart, which is directly relevant to the question of how much we can trust self-reports.

I don't think it settles anything about moral status. It doesn't tell you whether there's any experience there. But it's the right kind of evidence to be gathering. If we're ever going to make progress on these questions, it's going to be through understanding the mechanisms, and this is about as good a window into the mechanisms as currently exists. It's also just very readable. It's long, but the case studies are written so you can follow them without a deep technical background, and I think most people come away with their intuitions somewhat scrambled in a productive way.

r001.rationale: It connects evidence about model internals to the speaker’s AI welfare questions, including how the findings bear on trust in model self-reports.

r002.rationale: It describes attribution graphs as tracing internal features and connections involved in producing a response, which matches the criterion’s description of investigating output-generation processes.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really fascinating window into what’s actually happening inside these systems. We’re used to interacting with a language model by typing something in and reading what comes out. But that leaves a huge amount unanswered about how it arrived at that response. This paper starts to trace some of those internal computations, giving us something more concrete than intuitions based on how humanlike the output sounds.

From the perspective of AI welfare, that’s a direction I’m particularly excited about. The paper isn’t a test for consciousness, and finding sophisticated internal processes doesn’t establish that a model has experiences. But if we want to make progress on those questions, we need to understand what these systems are actually doing internally. I’d recommend it as a glimpse of what that kind of investigation can look like.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper traces internal computations and connects understanding model internals to progress on AI welfare questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really useful way to get a more concrete picture of what’s going on inside these systems. We tend to interact with a language model through this very narrow interface: you type something in, and it produces words. And it’s easy to jump from that to a story about what it’s thinking, based on how a person might have produced those words.

The paper tries to look under the hood and trace some of the actual mechanisms producing the behaviour. And you get this picture that’s much stranger and more interesting than either “it’s basically a person” or “it’s just autocomplete” would suggest.

From the perspective of thinking about AI consciousness or welfare, I wouldn’t say it settles those questions. But understanding what these systems actually do internally seems like a crucial part of making progress on them. That’s why I recommend it.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper traces mechanisms inside models and that understanding those internals is crucial for progress on AI consciousness or welfare.

r002.rationale: It describes looking under the hood to trace the mechanisms producing model behavior, which communicates investigating internal processes behind outputs.
